title: Why the Bank of England raised rates before wage pressure was conclusive
summary: The Bank of England’s November Monetary Policy Report asks how far an energy shock can lift prices before it also changes the way firms set prices and workers bargain over pay. At its November meeting the Committee raised Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. Direct energy effects had already raised inflation, recent activity had exceeded expectations and some of the costs facing households and businesses had yet to appear on their bills. Staff still saw limited evidence of persistent wage and price feedback. The report sets out the evidence behind acting before that distinction could be resolved, and scenarios for what would happen if the Committee’s central judgement proved wrong (overview and §3).

September CPI inflation was 3.5%, up from 2.6% in June and 0.4 percentage points above July’s projection. Household energy and motor fuels accounted for about 60% of the excess above the 2% target. That proportion refers to the overshoot relative to target. Constraints on refining had kept refined-product margins unusually high for diesel and jet fuel. The UK gas futures path used for the forecast averaged about 65% above its July counterpart. As regulated household tariffs reset, an increase already visible in wholesale prices could lift consumer prices months later. Staff projected CPI inflation of 4.9% in the second quarter of 2027 (§1.1, Charts 1.1–1.6).

Fixed-price energy contracts and hedges protected some firms for a time. Other businesses absorbed higher bills by accepting lower margins. Both responses can suppress measured pass-through initially while leaving prices exposed when contracts expire or margins come under further pressure. In Box A, energy-intensive firms expected faster increases in their selling prices. The forward-looking markers in Chart A.1 are firm expectations rather than completed price changes. Private-sector regular earnings grew about 3% in August, whereas two other wage indicators suggested around 4%. Changes in the mix of employers and jobs accounted for part of the gap. The report’s dashboard records elevated household attention to inflation alongside more stable survey evidence on the connection between wage and selling-price expectations (§1.1, Box A and Table A.1).

The growth evidence also admits more than one interpretation. Business-to-business services supplied roughly 0.6 percentage points of the 0.7% quarterly growth in the three months to August. An industry proxy attributed just under one fifth of growth since the start of 2026 to new AI-related activity, but the industries measured also produce other goods and services. Strong demand in those sectors and a lasting increase in productive capacity would imply different pressures on prices. Mortgage transmission was similarly uneven. New two-year fixed quotes at 75% and 90% loan-to-value had risen about 60 basis points on average since July, with the effect on outstanding borrowers arriving as loans reset (§§1.2–1.3 and Boxes C–E).

Tables 3.A and 3.B compare outcomes under the same market interest-rate path. Central four-quarter CPI inflation was 4.0% in 2027 Q4 and 2.0% in 2028 Q4. More persistent energy prices and stronger wage and price feedback in the adverse scenario lifted the corresponding rates to 5.5% and 3.0%. Under weaker demand the same energy path as in the central projection produced 3.6% and 1.2%. These conditional paths carry no probabilities. The additional policy-rule exercises ask a separate question about how rates might respond to each economic outcome. The projected inflation differences in the common-rate experiment show why energy futures alone cannot establish how long UK policy should remain restrictive (§3, Charts 3.1–3.7 and Annex 1).

questions.question: Which observations would distinguish deferred energy pass-through from a broader change in wage and price setting?
questions.detail: Match employers’ energy contract expiry dates with realised sales prices, margins and dated pay settlements. Compare businesses with similar demand but different renewal dates, and test whether prices and pay still adjust together after allowing for energy intensity. Use the Decision Maker Panel and Agents’ contact records to check whether firms’ earlier intentions predicted actual behaviour.

questions.question: How much of the upward-sloping forward curve represents expected policy and how much represents risk compensation?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the precise 15-working-day market window used for Chart 1.15, then compare dated transactions with the Bank’s survey fieldwork and its distributions at common horizons. Use additional option and forecast evidence to assess plausible decompositions. Differences in timing, respondent selection and the distinction between a modal survey response and a forward rate limit a direct subtraction.

questions.question: Which borrowers will have to refinance after exhausting their savings buffer?
questions.detail: Link mortgage reset schedules and original loan terms with household liquid assets and spending where access permits. Check whether the change in effective payments is followed by lower spending, additional borrowing or arrears, distinguishing borrowers who refinance soon from those still protected by earlier fixed rates. Compare these groups with the aggregate path in the projections databank.
